reviews.quote: The Trial Court found that although the plaintiff had failed in proving his title, he had succeeded in proving his possession over the suit property which he was entitled to protect unless dispossessed therefrom by due process of law.
reviews.reason: R1 faithfully represents the distinction between establishing possession and proving proprietary title. The Supreme Court reports that the Trial Court found the plaintiff's possession proved while his title remained unproved, and subsequently endorses deciding the injunction claim on possession without resolving ownership. The ALL connective appropriately combines these two reported findings concerning the same plaintiff and identified suit property. The conclusion is limited to preserving an independent basis for possessory protection; it does not automatically establish entitlement to an injunction or determine ownership. The permitted finding statuses correctly distinguish judicial findings from allegations and independently verified evidence. Failure to prove title is not converted into proof that the plaintiff lacks ownership or that the defendant owns the property. No independent burden allocation or evidentiary standard is introduced. The absence of exception slots is acceptable because this rule preserves a basis for further evaluation rather than granting unconditional protection. Its scope limitations appropriately reserve the disputed boundaries and the additional settled-possession inquiry.

reviews.quote: It is the settled possession or effective possession of a person without title which would entitle him to protect his possession even as against the true owner.
reviews.reason: R2 accurately captures the legal protection of peaceful and settled possession, including possession unsupported by established ownership. The judgment distinguishes effective, settled possession from merely stray, intermittent, casual, or incipient trespass. It recognizes protection against forcible interference by even a rightful owner while permitting legally appropriate resistance to a fresh or incomplete intrusion and preserving judicial recovery. OPEN_TEXT is the correct connective because the judgment expressly resists a rigid formula for classifying settled possession. The reported considerations concerning physical occupation, duration, effectiveness, disturbance, owner knowledge, concealment, possessory intention, completed dispossession, acquiescence, and cultivation are context-sensitive rather than a universally sufficient mechanical conjunction. The transient-trespass exception is material. Its expected FALSE value is defensible only as a consequence of accepting the Supreme Court's reported characterization of the plaintiff's possession as settled; it is not an independently established historical finding about every act of occupation. R2 expressly preserves that distinction and identifies the underlying semantic evaluation as unimplemented. The R1 input narrows the rule to this reconstruction without purporting to define every situation in which settled possession may be protected. The conclusion does not establish the defendant's ownership. The rule correctly avoids inventing a numerical duration, universally mandatory crop requirement, or independent burden standard.

reviews.quote: The law will come to the aid of a person in peaceful and settled possession by injuncting even a rightful owner from using force or taking law in his own hands
reviews.reason: R3 faithfully connects legally protectable settled possession with a possessory basis for injunctive restraint against attempted interference. The Supreme Court recounts that the defendant obstructed the plaintiff's construction while asserting ownership, and endorses protection of the plaintiff's established possession against interference. The ALL connective appropriately requires both a protectable possessory interest and relevant interference with the same property by the identified opponent. The defendant's assertion of ownership remains separate from proof of ownership, and the recorded obstruction does not independently establish that physical force was used. The conclusion is appropriately limited to an independent legal ground for injunction, not automatic satisfaction of every procedural or discretionary requirement. The rule preserves lawful recovery through appropriate proceedings and inherits R2's distinction between settled possession and transient trespass. Its lack of separate exception slots is acceptable within that expressly limited conclusion. No unsupported burden allocation, finding of proprietary title, or independent execution of R2's open-text evaluation is introduced.

reviews.quote: In Kallappa Rama Londa's case, the learned Single Judge has upheld the maintainability of a suit merely seeking injunction, without declaration of title
reviews.reason: R4 accurately reconstructs the Supreme Court's rejection of the defendant-appellant's contention that failure to establish title or omission of declaratory relief necessarily defeated the injunction claim. The judgment expressly rejects both submissions, distinguishes the Allahabad decision concerning discretionary temporary injunction, and endorses the proposition that an independently supportable possessory claim need not fail solely because title remains unresolved. The ALL connective appropriately combines the derived possessory basis with the fact that the specified title-related objection was raised in this litigation. The second input is correctly designated PARTY_CLAIM: it records counsel's arguments without independently establishing the precise contents or defects of the pleadings. The conclusion is carefully expressed as the absence of an automatic bar, rather than universal maintainability of every injunction-only action involving disputed title. The scope limitations appropriately distinguish merits-stage adjudication from interim discretionary relief and avoid independently attributing all factual conditions from cited precedents to this case. No general procedural test for declaratory relief, independent verification of the cited decisions, or unsupported burden allocation is asserted. The conclusion remains grounded in possession rather than confirmation of ownership.

reviews.quote: Legal remedies thus appointed for the protection of possession even against ownership are called possessory, while those available for the protection of ownership itself may be distinguished as proprietary.
reviews.reason: R5 faithfully represents the central distinction between possessory and proprietary protection. The Supreme Court invokes the jurisprudential distinction, relates it to Indian law, and expressly clarifies that the impugned judgment does not determine title for or against either litigant. The single-input ALL connective is sufficient for the narrow non-entailment conclusion: an independent possessory basis for injunctive relief does not itself establish ownership. This does not mean possession can never have evidentiary significance for title. The judgment separately recognizes possession or prior peaceful settled possession as evidence of title in the absence of better proof and discusses a rebuttable presumption relating possession to title. R5 properly distinguishes such evidentiary significance from conclusive proprietary adjudication. Its conclusion also does not establish that the opposing party lacks ownership or that independent proprietary adjudication is impossible. The absence of exception slots is appropriate for this limited logical distinction, while the scope limitations preserve the possibility of separate title proceedings. The rule does not invent a conclusive evidentiary presumption, determine the disputed boundary, or introduce an unsupported burden standard.

reviews.quote: It is still open to the defendant-appellant to file a suit based on his title against the plaintiff-respondent and evict the latter on the former establishing his better right to possess the property.
reviews.reason: R6 accurately preserves the separate proprietary route expressly recognized by the Supreme Court. The judgment states that the Trial Court left title open, records that the defendant also failed to establish title sufficient to support his claimed entitlement to evict the plaintiff, and confirms that both parties remain free to establish their respective claimed titles in duly constituted proceedings. The ALL connective combines the distinction established by R5, the express reservation of title, and the defendant's reported non-proof of title. These conditions provide a sufficient case-specific context for the conclusion; the defendant's earlier failure of proof must not be interpreted as a universal prerequisite for bringing a later proprietary action. The conclusion appropriately distinguishes permission to seek adjudication from present entitlement to possession or guaranteed success in later proceedings. It preserves the express condition that a claimant seeking title-based eviction establish a better right to possess the property. That condition does not establish either party's title now or authorize self-help dispossession. The scope limitations correctly exclude future procedural admissibility, limitation questions, unknown evidence, and unresolved land demarcation. Although the judgment identifies the need to establish a better right, the rule does not invent additional burden-shifting provisions or standards of proof. The final appellate disposition is not used as an antecedent.

coverage_limits: All six candidate rules were reviewed against the complete supplied Supreme Court judgment in Case 789051, Rame Gowda (D) by Lrs. v. M. Varadappa Naidu (D) by Lrs. & Anr., decided on 15 December 2003. Acceptance means fidelity as a research translation for the specified issue and stage, not qualified legal approval or independent validation of the underlying findings.

The review addresses the Supreme Court merits appeal and the distinction between protection of established possession and confirmation of ownership. It does not reconstruct every legal issue, possible cause of action, remedy, or procedural requirement arising from the litigation.

The original plaintiff-respondent and defendant-appellant are the relevant opposing roles. Their claimed adjoining parcels are not assumed identical. The protected property is the particular suit schedule land at Arekempanahally, 36th Division; the precise boundaries, dimensions, and competing proprietary claims remain unresolved.

The Trial Court's reported findings of proved plaintiff possession and unproved plaintiff title, together with the Supreme Court's reported settled-possession characterization and finding of defendant title non-proof, are accepted only under the supplied reconstruction policy. The underlying evidence and lower-court records were not independently examined.

The defendant-appellant's objections concerning failure to establish title and omission of declaratory relief are treated as reported party arguments. Recording those objections does not establish their legal correctness or independently verify every allegation about the original pleadings.

R2 contains an explicitly unimplemented OPEN_TEXT legal evaluation. The supplied judgment does not permit independent verification of every factor relevant to settled possession, including occupation duration, owner knowledge, acquiescence, possessory intention, and completion of dispossession. Its reported settled-possession classification is not a substitute for a fully executed factual test.

The exception concerning merely casual, intermittent, stray, or incipient trespass remains material. The expected absence of that classification rests on the Supreme Court's contrary settled-possession finding, not independent proof that no temporary or incomplete intrusion ever occurred. The judgment also recognizes legally permissible resistance to fresh intrusion and distinguishes recovery through due process.

The defendant's obstruction of construction is reported in the judgment. This does not independently demonstrate the use of physical force, prove the defendant's asserted ownership, or establish the precise disputed boundary.

The judgment's recognition that possession may provide evidence of title does not amount to conclusive confirmation of ownership. Neither party's failure to prove title is equivalent to a definitive finding that the party lacks any proprietary right.

R4 concerns the insufficiency of title-related objections as automatic grounds for dismissal of an otherwise supportable possessory injunction claim. The judgment distinguishes a precedent concerning discretionary temporary injunction, and the review does not generalize that distinction into a comprehensive procedural rule for all injunction-only suits.

R6 recognizes a case-specific route to later proprietary proceedings. Its ALL connective expresses sufficient circumstances for the selected reconstruction, not universally necessary conditions for future title litigation. No future title finding, successful suit, possession decree, or eviction is inferred.

The obligation to establish a better right to possession before obtaining the contemplated title-based eviction is preserved from the judgment. Beyond that express condition, burden allocation and standards of proof remain NOT_COVERED. No additional evidentiary or procedural burden is invented.

The cited precedents, Salmond's jurisprudential discussion, original pleadings, exhibits, testimony, and lower-court judgments were not independently consulted. Their content is considered only insofar as it is described or adopted in the supplied Supreme Court judgment.

The Supreme Court's dismissal of the appeal and its treatment of the lower-court injunction are available solely for comparison with the reconstructed reasoning. The final disposition is not used as a premise establishing any rule or as circular support for the requested conclusion.

The candidate registry has not been silently rewritten. Each acceptance is confined to its recorded premises, conclusion strength, connective interpretation, exceptions, scope restrictions, and express unimplemented evaluations. Broader legal validity and implementation of omitted legal or factual assessments remain outside this source review.
